title: THE VERSE ABOUT “TREASURES IN HEAVEN” WE KEEP READING—BUT MAY HAVE NEVER REALLY HEARD
paragraphs:
THE VERSE ABOUT “TREASURES IN HEAVEN” WE KEEP READING—BUT MAY HAVE NEVER REALLY HEARD
Jesus Wasn't Teaching You How to Become Rich in Heaven. He Was Exposing What Already Owns Your Heart.
There is a terrifying possibility hidden inside one of Jesus’ most familiar sayings.
You can spend your entire life collecting things you cannot keep…
while neglecting the things you can never lose.
You can build the house.
Grow the savings.
Protect the reputation.
Buy the things you once prayed you could afford.
Become respected.
Become comfortable.
Become successful.
And still wake up one day and discover that somewhere along the road, without realizing it…
your possessions stopped belonging to you.
And you started belonging to them.
That is why the words of Jesus in Matthew 6 are far more unsettling than they first appear.
Jesus says:
“Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth… but store up for yourselves treasures in heaven… For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
Matthew 6:19–21
We have heard those words so often that they can slide across the surface of the soul without penetrating it.
But listen again.
Jesus is talking about your heart.
Not merely your wallet.
Not merely your possessions.
Not merely how much money you give away.
Your heart.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part of His warning is this:
You may not have to ask where your heart is.
You may only have to look at where your treasure keeps going.
The Greek of Matthew makes Jesus’ wording striking.
“Μὴ θησαυρίζετε ὑμῖν θησαυροὺς…”
Mē thēsaurizete hymin thēsaurous…
Then:
“θησαυρίζετε δὲ ὑμῖν θησαυροὺς ἐν οὐρανῷ…”
thēsaurizete de hymin thēsaurous en ouranō…
The wording deliberately repeats the same word family.
Thēsaurizō means to store up, accumulate, or treasure.
Thēsauros means treasure, a store of wealth, something laid up as valuable.
In other words, Jesus’ language carries the force of:
Do not keep treasuring up treasures for yourselves on earth.
Instead…
treasure up treasures in heaven.
And then Jesus tells us why.
“ὅπου γάρ ἐστιν ὁ θησαυρός σου, ἐκεῖ ἔσται καὶ ἡ καρδία σου.”
Hopou gar estin ho thēsauros sou, ekei estai kai hē kardia sou.
“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
Matthew 6:21
Notice something extraordinary.
Jesus does not merely say that your treasure follows your heart.
He warns that your heart follows your treasure.
That changes the question.
Because we often imagine:
“I care about this, therefore I invest in it.”
Jesus makes us confront the other direction too:
“What I continually invest myself in can capture my heart.”
Think about that.
Every purchase.
Every sacrifice.
Every hour.
Every obsession.
Every ambition.
Every quiet act of generosity.
Every secret act of obedience.
Every opportunity to help somebody that nobody else notices.
Every time you choose Christ over applause.
Every time you choose integrity when compromise would have paid better.
Every time you give when nobody will post your name.
Every time you forgive when revenge would feel better.
Every time you quietly help someone who cannot repay you.
Every time you surrender something because Jesus is worth more.
Something is happening inside you.
Your treasure is moving.
And your heart is moving with it.
That is why “treasures in heaven” cannot faithfully be reduced to a heavenly investment scheme where Christians perform good deeds so God will make them cosmically wealthy.
Jesus is confronting something much deeper.
He is confronting allegiance.
Look at what comes only a few verses later.
“No one can serve two masters.”
And then Jesus names them:
God and money.
Matthew 6:24.
Suddenly the entire passage becomes sharper.
Jesus moves from treasure…
to heart…
to vision…
to masters.
This is not primarily financial advice.
This is discipleship.
This is worship.
This is a question of who owns you.
Money itself is not the villain.

Scripture does not teach that possessing material resources automatically makes someone ungodly. Abraham possessed wealth. Job possessed wealth. There were people who used their resources to serve Jesus and His mission.
The danger is not merely having something.
The danger is when something has you.
That is why a person can have very little money and still worship money.
And another person can possess considerable resources while holding them with an open hand before God.
Greed is not measured only by the amount in your bank account.
Sometimes greed lives inside the sentence:
“If I just had a little more, then I would finally be okay.”
A little more.
Then a little more.
Then a little more.
Until “enough” becomes a destination you never reach.
Jesus knew what we spend decades discovering.
Earthly treasure makes promises it cannot keep.
The moth comes.
Decay comes.
Thieves come.
Markets change.
Businesses collapse.
Possessions break.
Beauty fades.
Bodies age.
Careers end.
Applause moves to somebody else.
People forget your accomplishments.
Eventually, someone else will live in the house you fought to own.
Someone else may drive what you polished.
Someone else will sort through the belongings you were convinced you needed.
And one day your name itself may become a photograph in somebody else’s drawer.
Jesus is not being morbid.
He is setting us free.
He is looking at frightened human beings desperately trying to construct permanence out of temporary materials and saying:
There is another Kingdom.
There is another treasure.
There is something death cannot touch.
This becomes even clearer when Jesus teaches the same truth elsewhere.
In Luke 12, He connects heavenly treasure with generosity—giving to those in need and seeking a treasure that does not fail.
Later, Paul tells wealthy believers not to put their hope in uncertain riches, but in God, and to be rich in good works, generous, and ready to share, thereby laying up treasure for the future.
The biblical picture is remarkably consistent.
Heavenly treasure is connected to a life redirected toward God’s Kingdom.
Generosity.
Faithfulness.
Mercy.
Obedience.
Love.
Sacrifice.
Good works flowing from genuine faith.
Resources surrendered to God rather than worshiped as god.
But we must protect the Gospel here.
You cannot buy heaven.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
You cannot donate enough money to erase your sins.
The Gospel destroys that illusion.
We are sinners who need mercy.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose from the dead.
Salvation is received by grace through faith, not purchased through religious performance.
Jesus is the treasure before anything we could ever do for Him becomes treasure.
That distinction matters.
Otherwise “store up treasures in heaven” becomes another religious marketplace.
Give this much.
Do these things.
Earn this reward.
Make God impressed with you.
No.
Christian obedience does not begin with us trying to purchase God’s acceptance.
It begins with realizing that in Christ, grace has come looking for people who could never purchase it.
And once grace reaches the heart…
the hands begin to open.
Maybe that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because there are things we say we love…
and then there are things our lives reveal that we treasure.
We say Jesus matters most.
But look at our attention.
We say eternity matters.
But look at our anxiety.
We say people matter more than possessions.
But sometimes we destroy relationships protecting things.
We say God provides.
Yet sometimes losing money frightens us more than losing intimacy with God.
We say we want our children to know Christ.
Yet we can spend enormous energy building their earthly future while barely thinking about their souls.
We say the Gospel is priceless.
Yet sometimes we are embarrassed to share it because someone might think differently of us.
That is where Jesus’ words stop being a Bible quotation hanging beautifully on a wall.
They become a mirror.
Where is your treasure?
Not where should it be.
Not where do you tell people it is.
Where is it?
Look at what receives your deepest attention.
Look at what you are terrified to lose.
Look at what controls your decisions.
Look at what you constantly imagine possessing.
Look at what makes you feel important.
Look at what you protect at almost any cost.
Look at what you would struggle most to surrender if Jesus put His finger on it tonight.
There may be your treasure.
And somewhere nearby…
there is your heart.
This does not mean Christians should never save money, own homes, build businesses, prepare for emergencies, buy beautiful things, or provide responsibly for their families.
Scripture commends wisdom, responsibility, provision, diligence, and generosity.
The issue Jesus exposes is not responsible stewardship.
It is ultimate allegiance.
Earthly possessions make wonderful servants.
They make terrible gods.
Because every earthly treasure eventually whispers the same lie:
“Keep me, and you will be safe.”
Jesus says something infinitely better:
Seek first the Kingdom of God.
Your security was never supposed to rest in what you can accumulate.
It rests in the Father who knows what you need.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly what it feels like to discover that earthly treasure cannot save you.
You lost the job.
You watched the business fail.
You buried someone you would have traded every possession to keep.
You finally bought what you thought would make you happy…
and the emptiness came home with you.
You reached the milestone.
Everyone congratulated you.
Then that night, when the noise disappeared, you were still alone with your soul.
And suddenly you understood something nobody could have taught you in a classroom.
Having more is not the same thing as having life.
That may be why Jesus’ teaching is not bad news for the wealthy or romanticism for the poor.
It is liberation for everyone.
The poor person does not have to become rich to become eternally rich in Christ.
The wealthy person does not have to be possessed by what he possesses.
The ashamed can be forgiven.
The greedy can repent.
The selfish can become generous.
The frightened can learn trust.
The person who wasted decades chasing what disappears can still turn around.
That is grace.
And grace means your past does not get the final sentence.
Maybe you spent years building your kingdom.
Jesus can still teach you to seek His.
Maybe money became your identity.
Jesus can give you another name.
Maybe success became your savior.
Jesus can expose the idol without abandoning the idolater.
Maybe you have been selfish.
Repentance is still possible.
Maybe you have wasted opportunities to love people because you were too busy collecting things.
There is mercy at the cross.
This is what Jesus does.
He takes people whose treasure has been buried in all the wrong places…
and gives them a new heart.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And when Christ begins rewriting a person, generosity stops being merely an obligation.
It becomes evidence that something has happened inside.
You begin seeing money differently.
Time differently.
Possessions differently.
People differently.
Eternity differently.
You begin asking a question the world rarely teaches us to ask:
“How can what God entrusted to me serve something that will outlive me?”
Maybe that means feeding somebody.
Supporting Gospel ministry.
Caring for a widow.
Helping a struggling family.
Giving quietly.
Opening your home.
Funding missions.
Supporting faithful Christian teaching.
Giving away a book that brings someone closer to Scripture.
Sitting beside someone who is grieving.
Teaching your child the Gospel.
Forgiving someone.
Serving when nobody applauds.
Sharing Christ with the person everyone else has written off.
Standing beside a believer who is barely holding onto hope.
Not because these actions purchase salvation.
Because salvation changes what we treasure.
There is an enormous difference.
We do not give so Jesus will love us.
We give because in Christ we have encountered a love money could never buy.
We do not serve to purchase heaven.
We serve because our citizenship has been redirected toward heaven.
We do not perform good works to replace the cross.
Good works flow from lives captured by the One who died on that cross.

And that means even something as ordinary as sharing this article can become meaningful—not because clicking “Share” earns heavenly credit, and certainly not because God needs social media statistics—but because truth is meant to travel.
Somebody on your Facebook friends list may be quietly falling apart.
Somebody may have everything except peace.
Somebody may be chasing money because nobody has told them that money makes a terrible messiah.
Somebody may be ashamed of what they have become.
Somebody may believe they have wandered too far from Christ to return.
Not for an algorithm.
Not for religious applause.
Not to prove anything to God.
There is treasure the grave cannot steal.
Send this privately to the friend who has been exhausted by chasing success.
What earthly treasure has been hardest for you to surrender to God?
You do not need to tell your entire story.
Even three words may be enough.
“Jesus, change me.”
“Teach me surrender.”
“Pray for me.”
“I’m still fighting.”
“No more hiding.”
Or perhaps:
“Christ is my treasure.”
Your honesty may become the permission somebody else needed to stop pretending.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, confront sin, understand grace, heal, repent, and grow deeper in Jesus Christ, you can follow and stay connected for daily biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment.
There are people who will never walk through the doors of a church because someone tells them to.
But they may read something you share at 1:17 in the morning when their life has finally become quiet enough for their soul to listen.
Never underestimate what God can do with truth placed in front of someone at the right moment.
It does not make you more saved.
It does not purchase heavenly treasure.

It is simply a practical, voluntary way to support the continued work of putting Christ-centered biblical teaching into more hands while receiving deeper opportunities for Christian nourishment and discipleship.
You are not less important.
God's grace is not behind a paywall.
Because the goal was never merely to create supporters.
The goal is disciples.
People who know Jesus.
People who treasure Jesus.
People who stop building their identity around things moths can eat, decay can destroy, thieves can steal, markets can erase, and death can take away.
People who finally understand that Christianity is not about adding Jesus to a crowded treasure chest.
It is discovering that Jesus is worth more than the chest.
So imagine something.
Imagine the final evening of your earthly life.
The room is quiet.
Your achievements cannot speak.
Your possessions cannot hold your hand.
Your bank balance cannot add another heartbeat.
The titles people gave you cannot enter eternity beside you.
The house stays behind.
The clothes stay behind.
The phone stays behind.
The account stays behind.
The trophies stay behind.
Everything this world taught you to call “mine” begins slipping from your hands.
And suddenly only one question matters:
What did you treasure?
Not what did you own.
What owned your heart?
That is why Jesus’ warning is actually mercy.
He is telling us now.
Before the moth.
Before the decay.
Before the thief.
Before the funeral.
Before eternity.
He is telling us while there is still time to repent.
Still time to forgive.
Still time to become generous.
Still time to make the phone call.
Still time to help somebody.
Still time to stop worshiping success.
Still time to stop hiding.
Still time to surrender.
Still time to come home.
And above all…
still time to treasure Christ.
Because the greatest treasure of heaven is not merely something Jesus gives.
It is Jesus Himself.
The One who was rich beyond comprehension entered our poverty.
The sinless One carried the scandal of sinners.
The innocent One went to the cross.
The King wore thorns.
The hands that formed humanity were pierced by humanity.
The One we rejected offered forgiveness.
And the grave that appeared to have taken everything could not keep Him.
Christ rose.
That is the Gospel.
And suddenly “treasure in heaven” is no longer an abstract religious phrase.
It becomes the cry of a heart that has finally discovered what cannot be taken away.
You can lose money and still have Christ.
You can lose status and still have Christ.
You can lose applause and still have Christ.
You can lose possessions and still have Christ.
You can walk through grief and still have Christ.
And when this earthly life finally releases its grip on you…
you will still have Christ.
So perhaps the question is not:
“How much treasure have I stored in heaven?”
Perhaps tonight the deeper question is:
“Jesus… what have I been calling treasure that has been stealing my heart from You?”
Do not run from the answer.
Bring it to Him.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive grace where shame has kept you hiding.
Open your hands.
Reorder your life.
And treasure the One no thief can steal.
And comment something honest—not impressive.
“Jesus, change my treasure.”
“Christ is my treasure.”
“Pray for me.”
Or simply…
“I surrender.”
Because maybe the greatest tragedy would not be reaching the end of life with empty hands.
Maybe it would be reaching the end with full hands…
and discovering that everything you were holding had an expiration date.
Hold loosely what death can take. Hold desperately to the Christ death could not keep.
